title: Psalm 93: The LORD Reigns Above the Floods
summary: The psalm proclaims that the LORD reigns, robed in majesty and armed with strength, so that the world is firmly established. His throne has stood from long ago, and he himself is from all eternity. The floods and seas lift up their roaring voices, but the LORD on high is mightier than them all, and his testimonies are sure and his house adorned with holiness forever.
story: Psalm 93 is the first of the psalms in Book IV that announce “The LORD reigns” (Psalms 93 and 96 to 99, with Psalm 95 closely related). Its placement answers the crisis that closed Book III. Psalm 89 had lamented that David's throne was cast to the ground; Psalm 93 declares that God's own throne “was established long ago” and cannot be moved. The king in Jerusalem may fall, but the King of all has never ceased to reign. This is the heart of Book IV's response to exile and loss. The psalm also follows Psalm 92, whose central line was “You, O LORD, are exalted forever”, and it takes up that confession as a royal proclamation. It will be followed by Psalm 94's plea for God to act as judge, a reminder that God's reign is confessed while the world is still full of injustice.
historical:
The Hebrew text gives Psalm 93 no heading and no author. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, adds a heading assigning it to the day before the Sabbath, and the Mishnah (the Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200) confirms that the Levites sang this psalm in the Second Temple on the sixth day of the week (Mishnah Tamid 7:4). Some connect this with the sixth day of creation, when God completed the world and the psalm's claim that it cannot be moved was first true.

Its date is uncertain. Some scholars consider it one of the older psalms, pointing to its short, repetitive lines and its use of imagery shared with Canaanite poetry. In the 1920s the Norwegian scholar Sigmund Mowinckel proposed that psalms like this one were sung at an annual autumn festival in Jerusalem celebrating the LORD's enthronement as king. That theory has been widely debated: some scholars accept a version of it, while others argue that the Old Testament gives no direct evidence for such a festival and that the psalm proclaims God's eternal kingship rather than an annual renewal of it. Others read the enthronement psalms as a group compiled after the exile to affirm that God still reigns when Israel has no king.
cultural:
In the mythology of Israel's neighbors, the sea was a force of chaos that threatened the ordered world. Texts from the Canaanite city of Ugarit (thirteenth century BC) tell how the storm god Baal fought Yamm, whose names include Prince Sea and Judge River, and after defeating him was acclaimed king. Babylonian myth told of Marduk defeating the sea goddess Tiamat. Psalm 93 uses similar language, the floods and rivers lifting their voices, but there is no battle and no rival deity. The waters roar, and the LORD is simply greater. The sea is a creature, not a god.

The psalm pictures God as a king dressed for his coronation, robed in majesty and girded with strength as with a warrior's belt. His throne is not in a palace in Jerusalem but above the world, and his house, the temple, reflects his holiness. Testimonies were the solemn declarations of God's covenant will, especially the law given at Sinai; the two stone tablets were called the testimony and kept in the ark (Exodus 25:16). For a first reader, God's reign over the sea and his sure word in the temple belonged together.
literary: Psalm 93 is a hymn of God's kingship, often called an enthronement psalm. It is short and built on staircase parallelism, a pattern in which a line is repeated and extended step by step, a feature also found in Canaanite poetry. Verse 3 is the clearest example: “The floodwaters have risen, O LORD; the rivers have raised their voice; the seas lift up their pounding waves.” The verb to lift up is repeated three times as the waters rise higher and higher, and then verse 4 answers with a counter-staircase in which the LORD's majesty rises above them all. The psalm moves from the kingship of God (verses 1 and 2), to the challenge of the waters (verses 3 and 4), to the stability of God's word and house (verse 5). The word established frames the first half: the world is established, and God's throne is established.

outline.t: The LORD reigns, robed in majesty, from eternity
The floods lift their voice; the LORD is mightier
Sure testimonies and a holy house

doctrines.note: The psalm's opening words, “The LORD reigns”, are the center of Book IV. God's kingship is not established by any human dynasty or ritual; it is from eternity and cannot be overthrown.
The roaring seas, symbols of chaos in the ancient world, are under God's rule. Nothing that threatens the order of creation is beyond his power.
God's testimonies, his revealed word, are “fully confirmed”. The same God who rules the sea has spoken reliably to his people.

words.note: Malak, to reign or be king. The Hebrew phrase behind “The LORD reigns” can also be translated as the LORD has become king, or as the LORD is king. Those who hold the enthronement-festival theory favor the first; others emphasize that God's kingship is eternal, as verse 2 insists. Either way, it is a royal proclamation.

Nahar, river or flood. It appears three times in verse 3. In Ugaritic poetry, River was a title of the sea god who opposed Baal; here the rivers are simply waters that God outmatches. The repetition builds the sense of rising threat that God overcomes.

Edah, testimony. It refers to God's solemn covenant declarations, his laws and statutes. Verse 5 moves from God's power over the sea to the reliability of his word, as if to say that the same stability that holds the world holds his promises.

christ: The New Testament connects Jesus with God's rule over the waters. When Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea and they became calm, the disciples asked who this was that even the wind and the sea obey him (Mark 4:39-41). For readers who knew psalms like this one, the answer was striking: he was doing what the psalm says the LORD does. Hebrews applies to the Son the language of an eternal throne (Hebrews 1:8), and Revelation hears the great multitude cry that the Lord God Almighty reigns (Revelation 19:6), before John sees a new heaven and earth in which the sea is no more (Revelation 21:1). The psalm itself is not a prediction of Jesus; it proclaims God's kingship. The New Testament's claim is that in Jesus that kingship has come near, and that the one who stilled the storm shares the throne of the God who reigns above the floods.
questions: The psalm was sung when Israel's own kings had failed. How does it help to confess that God reigns when human leaders or institutions have let you down?
The floods lift up their voice, and the LORD on high is mightier. What roaring waters in your life or in the world seem most threatening right now?
Verse 5 moves from God's power to the reliability of his word. Why might these two belong together for someone trying to trust God?
